# Architecture decisions

Short records of the choices that shaped the project, with the trade-offs that were accepted. Newest ideas go at the bottom.

## 1. ORM: Drizzle (not Prisma)

**Decision:** Drizzle ORM with SQL migrations generated by `drizzle-kit`.

**Why:** It is SQL-first and type-safe with no code-generation step or query-engine binary, which keeps serverless cold starts small. The same query code runs on `postgres.js` (production) and PGlite (embedded dev/test database), which is what lets the whole app run with zero setup and lets integration tests execute the _real_ migrations against _real_ PostgreSQL. It also supports `CHECK` constraints, partial indexes and (later) PostGIS geometry columns natively.

**Trade-off:** Smaller ecosystem than Prisma; relations are written by hand in repositories. Accepted: the schema is small and the repository layer isolates it.

## 2. Coordinates: `numeric(9,6)` now, PostGIS later

**Decision:** `lat`/`lng` as `numeric(9,6)` (≈ 0.1 m) with range `CHECK`s. See [database.md](./database.md) for the upgrade path.

**Why:** Plain lat/lng covers every v1 query (pin display, distance via haversine in application code for a few hundred places). PostGIS adds an extension requirement on every host and local database for no v1 benefit. The upgrade is additive (a generated `geography(Point,4326)` column + GiST index), so nothing needs redesigning.

## 3. Owner authentication: single-owner credentials + TOTP, behind a small interface

**Decision:** `OWNER_EMAIL` + scrypt-hashed password + TOTP two-factor, HS256-signed session cookie (`jose`), server-side checks on every mutation.

**Why:** There is exactly one account and visitors never sign in. A hosted identity provider (Clerk, Auth0, Supabase Auth) is the _ideal_ answer for MFA, passkeys and recovery, but it needs an external account and keys before anything can run, and adds a vendor for one user. This implementation is ~250 lines, has no database table, supports MFA from day one, and is exercised by unit and end-to-end tests (including replay rejection of one-time codes and invalidation of sessions when the password changes).

**Trade-offs, stated plainly:** there is no passkey support and no self-service password recovery (re-run `npm run setup:owner`). Rate limiting is in-memory per instance, so on serverless hosts it is a brake rather than a guarantee. If those matter, replace `src/lib/auth/*` and `getOwnerSession()` with a provider; every caller goes through `assertOwner()` / `requireOwner()`, so the change is one module.

## 4. Caching: Cache Components (`use cache` + tags)

**Decision:** `cacheComponents: true`. Public reads are `'use cache'` functions tagged `places`, `trips`, `bucket-list`; owner actions call `updateTag()` so a publish is visible immediately. Scheduled publishing relies on a 15-minute `revalidate`.

**Trade-off:** `notFound()` for an un-prerendered `/places/[slug]` is thrown after the static shell has started streaming, so the HTTP status is 200 (with `noindex` and the friendly not-found UI) rather than 404. Prerendered slugs and `/api` routes are unaffected. Awaiting `params` outside Suspense would give true 404s but would lose the instant app shell; we chose the shell.

## 5. A zero-config development database: PGlite

**Decision:** When `DATABASE_URL` is unset outside production, the app boots an embedded PostgreSQL (PGlite, real Postgres compiled to WASM), persisted in `.data/pglite`, runs the migrations and (once) seeds clearly-labelled demo data. During `next build` it uses an in-memory copy because several build workers cannot share one data directory. Production **refuses to start** without `DATABASE_URL` (see `src/lib/startup.ts`).

## 6. Map: bundled "offline atlas" as the default basemap

**Decision:** MapLibre renders either a licensed provider style (`MAPTILER_PUBLIC_KEY` / `MAP_STYLE_URL`) or a bundled retro atlas built from Natural Earth country shapes (public domain). The atlas is also the automatic fallback if the provider fails or times out.

**Why:** The spec forbids demo tile servers in production and requires content to render even when tiles fail. A local atlas keeps the globe, pins, clusters and routes working with no keys and no third party. **Streets, POIs and labels require a licensed provider** — the UI says "Atlas view · country level" until one is configured.

## 7. Pins as sprites in one symbol layer

**Decision:** Pins and cluster badges are drawn on a canvas and registered through `setMissingStyleImageResolver`; places live in a clustered GeoJSON source. **Why:** no DOM marker per place, so hundreds of places stay smooth. **Trade-off:** emoji glyphs depend on the platform's emoji font; the always-present synchronised list is the accessible equivalent of the map.

## 8. Uploads: signed direct upload, then server-side processing

**Decision:** Browser → `POST /api/uploads/sign` → `PUT` straight to storage (presigned URL bound to the approved type and length) → `finalizeUploadAction` downloads the original, verifies the file signature, re-encodes with `sharp` to WebP (full + thumbnail + blur placeholder), writes the variants and **deletes the original**.

**Why:** Direct upload keeps large files off the serverless function; server-side processing is the only place EXIF/GPS stripping can be _guaranteed_ (client-side stripping is bypassable and nothing could verify it). Unit and end-to-end tests assert the stored files carry no EXIF.

**Trade-off:** `sharp` runs in the finalize request (≈ 1–3 s for a large photo). Fine for one owner.

## 9. Privacy: approximate locations and scheduled publishing

Places can be `approximate` (public pin rounded to ≈ 11 km, address hidden, no `geo` in structured data) and can be scheduled for later. Rounding happens in the mapper that builds every public view, so exact coordinates never leave the server.

## 10. Native `<dialog>` instead of a headless-UI library

Modals (menu, lightbox, confirmations) use the platform `<dialog>` element: the browser provides the top layer, inert background, focus containment, Esc / back-gesture dismissal and focus return. The mobile bottom sheet is intentionally _not_ a dialog: it must not block the map.

## 11. Fonts: self-hosted from npm

Fraunces (weight + SOFT axes, 62 kB) and DM Sans (37 kB) come from `@fontsource-variable/*` through `next/font/local`. No request to Google at build or run time; builds work offline. Latin subset only — other scripts fall back to system fonts.

## 12. Content-Security-Policy keeps `'unsafe-inline'` for scripts

A nonce-based policy would make every page dynamic and defeat static caching. We compensate with `object-src 'none'`, `base-uri 'self'`, `frame-ancestors 'none'`, `form-action 'self'`, a strict `connect-src`/`img-src` derived from the configured providers, and no user-authored HTML ever reaching the DOM (stories are Markdown rendered by `react-markdown` without raw HTML).

## 13. Demo content is data, not mock code

Sample places are real rows flagged `is_demo`: stamped **DEMO** in the UI, `noindex`, excluded from the sitemap, shown by default only in development, never silently mixed into stats (the passport says how many demo places it counts), and removable in one click from the dashboard or with `npm run db:purge-demo`.
